title: UNH Stock Tracks Hot Monthly Streak: Wall Street Cheers ‘Impressive’ Q2 And Sees Over 20% More Room To Run - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth Group, Inc. (UNH) are headed for their fourth monthly win as Wall Street turns more bullish after a large second-quarter (Q2) earnings beat and a sweeping increase to its 2026 outlook. UNH stock rose 1% on Friday, bringing its monthly gain to nearly 3%, while shares also finished the week marginally higher. BofA called UnitedHealth’s quarter “impressive,” noting that earnings beat consensus by 31% and guidance rose 12%. The firm raised its price target to $512, implying over 20% upside, while reiterating a ‘Buy’ rating and citing a “strong” quarter and broad-based outlook increase. Morgan Stanley was even more bullish, lifting its target to $529, implying a 24% upside. The firm said the Q2 beat and higher 2026 targets “validate its disciplined strategy and establish a stronger base for future growth.” Truist, Oppenheimer and KeyBanc each moved to $500 targets, implying a 17% upside. Truist highlighted top- and bottom-line beats, a better Medical Care Ratio, and improving expectations for UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health. Oppenheimer said that the company “handily” topped expectations, while KeyBanc said results “topped bullish expectations” and argued UnitedHealth could hit $30 in earnings per share (EPS) sooner than anticipated. Goldman Sachs and UBS both raised their targets to $490, implying a 15% upside. Goldman cited a “material” earnings beat, stronger Optum Health profitability and a larger-than-expected guidance increase. UBS said UnitedHealth was “making good progress with more to go.” Meanwhile, RBC Capital raised its target to $478, implying a 12% upside. It remained positive on the earnings beat and guidance hike but flagged investor concern around persistent commercial medical-cost pressure. UnitedHealth posted adjusted EPS of $6.38, beating the $4.92 consensus and rising from $4.08 a year ago. Revenue of $112.03 billion also topped estimates, while the medical care ratio improved to 86.7% from 89.4%. Additionally, the company raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to $19.50-$20 from more than $18.25, lifted UnitedHealthcare’s operating profit forecast to at least $12 billion, and increased Optum Health’s outlook to at least $2.2 billion. CEO Stephen Hemsley said UnitedHealth was “returning to form” as stronger performance disciplines took hold. He reaffirmed the company’s 13%-16% long-term earnings-growth target and doubled the 2026 buyback goal to at least $5 billion. Medicare Advantage drove the beat, with costs coming in below expectations. “Medicare delivered a strong second quarter,” UnitedHealthcare CEO Tim Noel said. Commercial plans remained the weak spot, with medical-cost trends above 11%. On the other hand, Optum said its tools added nearly 200,000 patient-facing hours, cut clinician cognitive burnout by 90%, and achieved a 96% first-pass approval rate for digital prior authorizations. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment was ‘extremely bullish’ amid ‘extremely high’ message volume. One user said, “$UNH the dark horse that everyone is not seeing is their integration of AI across all business functions which will MASSIVELY cut down their overhead.” Another user said, “$UNH In Hemsley we trust!!! But yea, I think 470 - 550 might be a good exit point just looking at the historical data. Honestly, I want to hold this for a year for tax efficiency but I don't want the same CMS nightmare again in 2027/1 or at least as long as trump is in power.” For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. In May, Burry sold all of his GameStop shares, saying the company's plan to buy eBay (EBAY) is too risky and added that the proposed $56 billion deal would leave GameStop with too much debt, making the company financially weaker over the long term. Burry had also said the company's current direction no longer matches his original investment thesis, which was based on GameStop using its cash to make disciplined acquisitions while maintaining a strong balance sheet. Since Burry’s exit, GameStop has seen developments including Cohen's decision to abandon a performance-based compensation package, shareholder approval to expand the company's authorized share count, and GameStop's acquisition of roughly 9.8% of eBay, up from 5%, using existing cash rather than debt. Replying to a user’s question about whether several recent developments had changed his investment thesis, Burry said the events do not affect his opinion because his primary concern is the company's broader strategic direction. “No, not much. This is about the wrong strategy in going after eBay. I can see why he wants it. But it is unlikely it works well for GME shareholders, I believe,” wrote Burry. GameStop stock edged 0.05% higher overnight, ahead of Monday. A subscriber asked if Burry has taken into account Lululemon Athletica’s softening demand in the U.S., including lower website traffic, declining app downloads, heavier discounting through its "We Made Too Much" section and increased promotional activity in stores in his analysis. In his response, Burry said he incorporates such developments into his research, but they are only part of a broader investment process. “Yes, but again, no real management, the stock has fallen a tremendous amount, really to a point where if there is an expectation LULU is remotely in its current form in 10 years it is a no-brainer,” said Burry. He has been advocating for Lululemon, projecting it as a “Patience Trade”, because the transition period before the new CEO takes over could delay major strategic changes. Burry believes Lululemon has become an overlooked value stock, arguing that investors are focusing too much on its recent setbacks and not enough on its long-term strengths. Another user said, “Over $1.99M insider buy!$LULU triggers an extreme value alert as corporate giants load the absolute bottom!” So far this year, while GME stock has gained 9%, LULU stock has crashed 44%. SpaceX (SPCX) shares rose 1% overnight heading into Monday after CEO Elon Musk dismissed a report claiming that the rocket and satellite company had placed a $52 billion order with Foxconn for Nvidia-powered AI servers. SPCX stock fell 5% on Friday, extending its weekly decline to 15%. “This is fake news,” Musk said on X in response to a post summarizing the reported agreement. Taiwan’s Economic Daily said that Hon Hai Precision Industry, better known as Foxconn, had secured its first contract to manufacture AI servers for SpaceX. According to the report, SpaceX was preparing to deploy more than 13,000 server racks built around Nvidia’s GB300 platform. The estimated $52 billion value was based on an assumed cost of $4 million per rack rather than a disclosed contract price. Citrini analyst Jukan said on X that Foxconn had displaced the dominance of Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computer in supplying AI server infrastructure to SpaceX. It also claimed deliveries would begin in late 2026 and continue into the first quarter of 2027. Chairman Young Liu has previously said Foxconn expects to capture more than 40% of the global AI server market, while shipments of advanced AI racks are projected to increase through the end of the year. A separate Wall Street Journal report on Friday said that SpaceX was in discussions with the U.S. Department of Defense about supplying data-center capacity worth several billion dollars for military AI workloads. The talks were said to be ongoing and could still fail to produce an agreement. SpaceX has also explored offering computing power to outside AI customers as it seeks to compete more directly with cloud infrastructure providers such as CoreWeave. In June, SpaceX also reached computing arrangements with Google and Anthropic. The Google deal covered access to about 110,000 Nvidia chips, while Anthropic secured capacity at the company’s Colossus 1 data center in Memphis. The potential Defense Department arrangement would deepen SpaceX’s already extensive relationship with the U.S. military. The Pentagon relies on the company for rocket launches, satellite communications and missile-tracking systems. It is also seeking more computing capacity as intelligence agencies and military units increase their use of AI. SpaceX employees have reportedly discussed selling computing capacity at prices designed to compete with established cloud and specialized AI infrastructure providers. The Pentagon, meanwhile, is seeking funding for a new AI Arsenal initiative centered on access to high-end chips and computing resources. The military has also approved multiple tech companies, including SpaceX, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle, for classified AI-related work. Korean stocks tumbled again on Monday, led by declines in chip giants Samsung and SK Hynix, setting the stage for another bout of the recent yo-yo trade, where weakness in Korean chip stocks spills over to U.S. semiconductor names and back again, ahead of a key week of U.S. tech earnings. South Korea’s Kospi as well as Samsung stock fell 4.3% each, while SK Hynix shares were down 4% in local afternoon time. The two stocks together account for roughly 60% of the Kospi’s market capitalization, making it one of the most concentrated major equity indices in the world. SK Hynix's U.S. listed stock declined 0.3% in the overnight session. As of the last close, they have declined by about 10% from the opening price on the first day of trading on Jul. 10. The Direxion Daily South Korea Bull 3X Shares (KORU), a three-times leveraged ETF tracking South Korea’s largest stocks, was down 2%. U.S. memory stocks Micron and SanDisk were holding in the green, rebounding after a dismal weekly performance. Citigroup on Monday downgraded the South Korean market to “neutral,” ending an overweight stance held since mid-2025 due to heightened market volatility, according to a report in South China Morning Post. The move was driven by extreme volatility in chip stocks and a reduced exposure to AI-themed trades. The firm added that it remains long-term bullish on AI, but has turned more cautious on Korea in the near term. Since the start of July, investors have been rotating out of semiconductor and AI infrastructure names and back into large-cap technology and software stocks, marking a shift after months of chip-led gains. Memory makers such as Micron, Samsung and SK Hynix, along with other AI hardware suppliers, have come under pressure as investors question whether the explosive AI infrastructure spending can continue at the same pace. Meanwhile, money has flowed into software and Big Tech names – including Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta – as investors seek companies that are better positioned to monetize AI through applications and services rather than infrastructure alone. The rotation also reflects profit-taking in richly valued chip stocks ahead of earnings season. Alphabet will be the first of the tech majors to report this season, with its announcement scheduled for Wednesday, followed by Intel the next day. GOOGL has gained 11% year to date, while INTC rallied 156%, underscoring how investors piled into chip stocks in 2026. Investors will closely watch for signs that AI-driven demand remains resilient and whether company outlooks justify the sector’s outsized gains. ARK Investment Management founder-CEO Cathie Wood cheered Eli Lilly’s $3.8 billion AtaiBeckley acquisition on Sunday, calling it a “well-deserved” payoff for shareholders and a validation of Christian Angermayer’s psychedelic vision. ATAI stock rose 1% on Friday, adding 40% over the past five sessions and marking its best week in more than a year. Shares, however, were dipping more than 1% in overnight trading heading into Monday. Wood highlighted on X the biotech company’s role in bringing psychedelic medicines closer to mainstream clinical use: “Not only a well-deserved return for ATAI shareholders, this transaction validates Christian’s heartfelt mission and vision,” Wood said. She called Angermayer’s work with ATAI “one of the biggest catalysts of the psychedelic renaissance,” adding that clinical trials are increasingly validating the potential of psychedelics in treatment-resistant depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and broader mental health conditions. Wood also credited Angermayer with backing the field long before psychedelic medicine became widely accepted, fashionable, or investable. “Long before psychedelics were accepted, fashionable, or investable, Christian’s life’s mission was to reactivate them and bring back hope and health for those who had lost both,” she said. Wood’s praise came after ARK Invest reduced its ATAI stake last week. The ARK Genomic Revolution ETF (ARKG) sold 1.12 million ATAI shares worth about $6.02 million. As of Friday, however, ARKG still held 3.19 million shares valued at $22.78 million, or 1.4% of the fund. Lilly was also ARKG’s seventh-largest holding, with 61,258 shares worth $71.62 million and a 4.4% weighting. Eli Lilly said last week that it would acquire AtaiBeckley for up to $3.8 billion for the psychedelic drug developer as it builds out its neuroscience pipeline. Under the deal, shareholders would receive $6.75 in cash per ATAI share, with Lilly committing $2.8 billion at closing and an additional $1 billion for future milestones. The deal marked a 26% premium to AtaiBeckley’s shareholders. The companies are targeting completion of the acquisition in the third quarter of 2026. The centerpiece of the deal is BPL-003, an intranasal psychedelic therapy being tested in late-stage studies for treatment-resistant depression. Jefferies has projected that the drug could eventually generate $1 billion to $2 billion in sales if the program succeeds. AtaiBeckley has said the first late-stage data are expected in early 2029. Angermayer reflected on the deal over the weekend in an X post, saying ATAI’s next phase is about commercialization rather than advocacy. “Ten years ago, psychedelics needed an evangelist. Today, they need commercialization,” he said. After first exploring psychedelics in 2014, Angermayer helped launch Compass Pathways and ATAI in 2017 and invested more than $100 million of his own capital in ATAI. The two companies later raised over $1.5 billion, went public and helped build clinical credibility for psychedelic medicine. Ondas, Inc.’s stock edged nearly 0.6% higher overnight heading into Monday after falling for seven straight weeks. Retail traders are now hoping for a recovery in drone stocks, while rising U.S.-Iran tensions raise expectations for increased defense demand and growth in autonomous technology. U.S.-Iran tensions increased over the weekend as the U.S. launched more strikes on Iran, targeting military capabilities. The conflict also resulted in the death of a third U.S. service member. Ondas’ stock has been under pressure as investors reacted negatively to capital raises and executive stock sales, overshadowing acquisitions aimed at expanding its autonomous defense capabilities. Earlier this month, Ondas announced a deal valued at $875.8 million to acquire DZYNE Technologies, a defense technology company specializing in unmanned aircraft systems. Following the transaction, management raised its 2026 revenue forecast to at least $525 million, up from an earlier estimate of $390 million. The company completed an underwritten share offering of 46 million shares that generated approximately $217 million to support its drone and defense initiatives. The additional stock supply pressured shares as investors adjusted to dilution concerns. Sentiment also weakened after CEO Eric Brock sold about $31.9 million worth of shares in June. Despite the stock decline, analysts maintain a positive outlook, with all eight analysts covering the stock recommending either a “Buy” or “Strong Buy” with an average price target of $19.81, according to Koyfin data. The new price target implies a whopping 203% upside to the stock’s last closing price. Investors are watching whether Ondas can convert its expanded defense portfolio into sustained revenue growth. Ondas has combined its defense-related businesses, including DZYNE and stratospheric technology provider World View, under the Ondas Sentinel division. The company is also integrating Palantir Technologies' (PLTR) SkyWeaver AI platform into its operations to boost battlefield data processing and defense software capabilities. Also, Ondas has reported more than $110 million in second-quarter orders, supported by demand for autonomous systems, counter-drone solutions and defense partnerships. title: Carsey Candidate Policy Forums - University of New Hampshire
content: New Hampshire voters are deciding two U.S. House races and a U.S. Senate seat on Nov. 3, and this fall, the Carsey School of Public Policy gave Granite Staters the chance to hear each candidate’s case. No debate, no 30-second ads, just a 35-minute moderated discussion. The Candidate Policy Forums started on Oct. 5 in Durham with nominees from the 1st Congressional District, Stefany Shaheen and Anthony DiLorenzo. The series ended in Concord on Oct. 7 with the nominees from the 2nd Congressional District, Maggie Goodlander and Lily Tang Williams. The timing of the series didn’t lend itself to a shared stage for the U.S. Senate race. Instead, Chris Pappas and John Sununu each sat down with Kevin Sullivan separately for a similar, recorded conversation. Regardless of location and modality, each candidate got the same format: one minute to make their opening case, ~30 minutes to discuss the issues New Hampshire families deal with every day, and 60 seconds to address the audience and close in their own words. Each conversation was moderated by Kevin Sullivan, a UNH alumnus, associate editor at The Washington Post, and a Pulitzer Prize winner. With Election Day around the corner, here’s what each conversation covered, and where to watch the full thing. Democrat Stefany Shaheen, a Portsmouth native, framed her campaign around affordability. She pointed to a New Hampshire resident who saw his home heating oil bill nearly double this year and argued that tariffs have hit the district's Main Street businesses particularly hard. She also leaned on her family's personal experience with the region's housing shortage, calling for expanded low-income housing tax credits and more permanently affordable development. Republican Anthony DiLorenzo, a Portsmouth business owner making his first run for office, argued Washington needs more people willing to solve problems without a partisan lens. On energy, he pushed for a new natural gas pipeline into New England and said he supports an "all of the above" approach, including nuclear power. On the Middle East conflict, he said it was time to bring American troops home, while on immigration, he called for reform that acknowledges New Hampshire employers' workforce needs without granting a path to citizenship for those who entered the country illegally. Incumbent Rep. Maggie Goodlander, a Democrat and Navy veteran, opened by calling it "the honor of my lifetime" to represent the district and centered her conversation on the cost of living, telling Sullivan that utility rate increases have gone unchecked for too long. She also made the case for congressional term limits, arguing that no one should treat the job as a career. Republican Lily Tang Williams, a naturalized U.S. citizen who left Communist China, called herself "the embodiment of the American dream" and spoke about the toll of rising costs on her own constituents, describing an 81-year-old still working full shifts to make ends meet. On energy, she cited families facing summer electric bills topping $800 a month. Notably, both candidates support term limits for Congress — one of several points where the conversations revealed common ground rather than conflict. Democrat Chris Pappas, a sitting congressman, centered his conversation on affordability and the influence of outside money in politics, noting he's been significantly outspent by dark-money groups backing his opponent. On artificial intelligence, he didn't mince words: citing a 10% estimate of existential risk, he called for Congress to regulate the industry rather than let it police itself. On energy, he pointed to New Hampshire's position "at the end of the transmission line" and the real cost of a recent home heating oil bill a constituent shared with him. Republican John Sununu, a former U.S. senator and congressman, leaned on his engineering and private-sector background, framing himself as a pragmatic problem-solver. On AI, he focused on protecting vulnerable populations — older Americans and minors — from fraud and exploitation. On energy, he called for expanded natural gas access and permitting reform. Notably, both Senate candidates said that U.S. involvement in the recent Middle East conflict was a mistake made without a clear plan, another moment where the two conversations lined up more than they diverged. title: Voices of UNH Manchester Wildcats Series: Meet Mechanical Engineering Technology Major, Kieran McCurdy, '25 - University of New Hampshire
content: Are you considering a future in mechanical engineering technology? Meet Kieran McCurdy, class of '25 at UNH Manchester, whose journey offers a firsthand look at the value of this dynamic program. Whether you’re a prospective student or simply curious about what makes UNH Manchester stand out, Kieran’s experience highlights the unique opportunities, hands-on learning, and career advantages waiting for you. For Kieran, the decision to attend UNH Manchester was driven by the program’s practical focus and its strong industry connections. He shares, “UNH Manchester is a hub for all these different companies. When you graduate, there are all these job opportunities that you can go into.” The campus’s location in the heart of Manchester, NH, puts students close to leading engineering firms and tech companies, opening doors to internships, networking, and career placement right after graduation. Kieran’s experience in the mechanical engineering technology program is marked by a diverse curriculum and hands-on learning. He explains, “My favorite thing about the mechanical engineering technology program at UNH Manchester is the array of classes you take. I get to learn about thermodynamics, electrical, and mechanical stresses all in one degree.” This means students gain expertise across multiple engineering disciplines, preparing them for a wide range of careers. Classes at UNH Manchester teach students not only theory; they also show them how to apply their knowledge in real-world situations. Kieran notes, “I’m taking a 3D printing class. With this class, I’ve been able to level up my 3D printing skills because I’m able to think more critically about the way I design.” The program’s modern facilities, including advanced labs and equipment, further support this hands-on approach. Highlights from Kieran’s Mechanical Engineering Technology Journey One of the highlights of Kieran’s journey was the capstone project, where he worked alongside fellow students to build robots. He explains, “You work on a team with three to four engineers, and you’re building robots. You’re required to make three 3D printed parts per robot and three machine parts per robot.” The project culminates in a friendly competition that lets students test their creations and celebrate their achievements. This experience encourages teamwork, critical thinking, and practical problem-solving. Kieran’s time at UNH Manchester has been filled with opportunities to apply his skills in real-world settings. As an automation intern at Freudenberg, Kerian gained valuable exposure: "We had an inspection machine there. I worked on the wire diagram for that machine," he shares. These internships, made possible by the campus’s industry connections, help students build their resumes and prepare for the workforce. Beyond the curriculum, Kieran appreciates the small class sizes and the collaborative environment. Faculty are invested in student success, and peers share a passion for innovation and problem-solving. The campus’s supportive community and access to advanced technology make it an ideal place to grow as an engineer. title: What can you do with sustainability? One alum’s journey led to graduate research on the state’s forest health - University of New Hampshire
content: Justin Wentworth ’26, who graduated with a dual degree in environmental sciences and sustainability, never dreamed he’d go to Cambodia. Added to the International Changemaker Grant student team just weeks before the trip, he said yes anyway, and it became a defining moment of his UNH experience. Now a graduate researcher at UNH, Justin is studying New Hampshire forest health through remote sensing. He reflects on the sustainability programs, campus experiences, and unexpected opportunities that shaped his journey. UNH grabbed my attention for its strong sustainability programming and campus living, as well as its natural resource programs and strong sense of community. I valued all of these things individually, but accumulatively, I could see my next steps in growth playing out in front of me. All on a packed campus that felt huge coming from my small town! In high school, my Environmental Sciences teacher and mentor Mrs. Howry pulled me into my focus area in and out of class, encouraging me to check out our sustainability club (that she helped run). The Society of Sustainable Spartans, or SOSS, laid the groundwork of my morals, values, and passion for protecting our planet. As a club we achieved successes I am forever fond of, such as upgrading our school's lighting system to LED's using funding from USDA. I knew I wanted to continue this path post high school and made this the core of my college search and how I spent my four-years at UNH. What were your most impactful undergrad experiences? In no particular order, my three most impactful experiences as an undergraduate at UNH were 1) my GIS capstone assessing water quality across India, 2) helping lead the Trash 2 Treasure program through the Sustainability Institute, and 3) my International Changemaker Grant trip to Cambodia. Tell us more about your trip to Cambodia through the International Changemaker Grant. My shoulder was tapped by a former group member when they had to drop out of the trip, and I didn't hesitate to find out more! The rest of the group found time to talk to me the very next day and I couldn't say no. The goal of the sustainability project directly connected with my own academic and research interests, giving me opportunity to display what I already know but even more so learn from fantastic peers and international professionals alike. I was beyond honored to join! This experience brought me a wave of growth. Professionally, I gained experience with various Geospatial Analysis tools, some I hadn't worked with before, and gave me experience not only presenting but teaching. This experience was the most direct, hands-on, out of the classroom opportunity related to environmental sciences, conservation work, and sustainability initiatives as an undergrad. It was my first trip outside of the country, or even on a plane! As such I was so radically moved by this trip. I feel more capable as an individual and more connected to our Earth. I was amazed by the culture of Cambodia and adored exploring Phnom Penh. Your trip involved a team of students from different majors; what was that experience like? Much of my time at UNH was spent surrounded by other natural resources mindset and methodology, as well as other sustainability folks. These are my people, but experiencing a few new lenses applied to an individual goal and project broadened my understanding. Particularly, how the coding / computer sciences, as well as humanitarian / social sciences can overlay geospatial analysis work. What should prospective students know about the International Changemaker Grant? I think the most unique perspective I can offer is my timeline of involvement in the project. I was added in very late, a reason to give a shout out and gratitude to my group members, who deserve most if not all of the credit, but it didn't dissuade their interest in me joining. I was about to graduate and would almost a month before the trip. I still went; it wasn't an issue. This is no small undertaking, but this is not the same as adding a 5th (or 6th) class to your course schedule. This is not taking on a part-time job. This is not committing to a semester abroad. If you have an interest at all, do not hesitate to try and fit this in. You won't regret it. This felt like the most fun, bonus cherry-on-top to my college experience. My graduate research is with the Basic and Applied Spatial Analysis Lab (BASAL) under Dr. Benjamin Fraser applying remote sensing tools to advance our state-level detection, tracking, and mitigation of forest pests like Emerald Ash Borer and Beech Leaf Disease. Our work will largely involve drone and satellite imagery, assessing forest health characteristics as well as effectiveness of current treatment plots for forest pests. New remote sensing methods have emerged, other projects have revealed successes and next steps with certain pests, and new technologies have become more efficient and/or readily available for industry and consumer use. At the same time, certain legislature changes have begun to reduce some options, creating extra navigational hurdles. We are charting a path forward in collaboration with the New Hampshire Agricultural Experimental Station to comply with new restrictions, test new methods, improve classification accuracies, and contribute to the larger interstate efforts to protect our forests from invasive pests. I am currently fully immersed with the geospatial analysis world, as you might expect given my research. For the next 2 years I know that my focus will be on my research, but I wouldn't have started into this next chapter without feeling a sense of calling and purpose to this field. It combines all of my academic and intellectual interests and allows me to fully "nerd out" regularly. It makes me understand and "trust the process" more and makes me wish I had somehow seen this pathway sooner. While that's out of my control, I hope to learn all I can in this field during my master's to guide my future, whether that is staying in academia or venturing outside of Durham to do similar work with state agencies or otherwise. I love this field so far! Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.
